title: EVG Supports Quantum Computing Development With Advanced Bonding Technology

content:
Semiconductor equipment maker EV Group (EVG) said on Nov. 10 that it will support quantum computing development using advanced packaging technologies, including bonding. The company aims to help increase qubit counts by integrating heterogeneous materials and devices into quantum chips based on various approaches, including trapped ions, superconducting circuits, photonics and spin qubits.

EVG is participating as a strategic partner of Silicon Austria Labs (SAL), which leads CHAMP-ION, a European project to establish a quantum chip pilot line. The company is also collaborating with Xanadu, a developer of photonic quantum computing technology, on research to address manufacturing requirements for emerging quantum devices.

In trapped-ion technology, EVG has developed a low-temperature metal bonding process to integrate ion-trap chiplets and photonic chiplets fabricated on different substrate materials. For superconducting quantum devices, it uses oxide-free bonding to enable superconducting interconnects and three-dimensional (3D) device integration. For photonic devices, EVG employs fusion bonding and oxide-free bonding to integrate materials such as III-V semiconductors into optical waveguides. For spin qubits, it applies hybrid bonding to enable ultra-high-density interconnections.

EVG uses its Heterogeneous Integration Competence Center (HICC) and NILPhotonics Competence Center to support customer process development and validation. HICC is equipped with wafer bonding, thin-wafer handling and lithography systems, supporting process development and pilot production for integrating heterogeneous materials and devices. The NILPhotonics center supports optical device development using nanoimprint lithography (NIL).

Quantum computing requires increasing qubit counts while maintaining performance and reliability. Qubits are the fundamental units of quantum information. Because quantum systems are particularly sensitive to errors, large numbers of physical qubits must be integrated to enable error correction. Different quantum computing approaches use different materials and device architectures, requiring high-density interconnections, heterogeneous material integration and precision manufacturing technologies.

"Quantum computing presents the challenge of integrating qubits into complex chip architectures without compromising performance, as each approach has different material and manufacturing requirements," said Bernd Dilacher, director of business development at EVG. "By leveraging EVG's diverse process technologies and experience in advanced packaging and heterogeneous integration, we can support customers in developing manufacturing processes for next-generation quantum devices."
